target_customer: Mobile app developers, from indie developers to larger studios, who needed a backend without running servers
problem: Every mobile app needed servers for data storage, push notifications and analytics, which meant backend work that small teams wanted to avoid.
business_model: Usage-tiered developer platform: free tier, paid plans by API requests, push notifications and storage (a $199 per month tier at launch), plus custom enterprise deals

founders.name: Kevin Lacker
founders.background_notes: Listed on the YC page. Wikipedia says the founders were previously at Google and Y Combinator.

founders.name: Ilya Sukhar
founders.background_notes: Per a TechCrunch Founder Stories summary, he entered YC as a solo founder and Paul Graham introduced him to Lacker; the team merged about a month into the batch.

founders.name: Tikhon Bernstam
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder by Wikipedia; not on the YC page.

founders.name: James Yu
founders.background_notes: Named as co-founder by Wikipedia; not on the YC page.

competitors.name: StackMob
competitors.what: Mobile backend as a service founded 2010
competitors.funding_then: Series A in May 2011 per a search summary of secondary sources

technical_complexity.rationale: Multi tenant cloud platform with SDKs for several platforms, hosted data store, push delivery and server side code execution, all run by a small team and scaled to thousands of developers.

defensibility.rationale: Apps built on the SDK and hosted data were costly to move, and word of mouth drove most signups. But the model was copyable and competitors existed from 2010.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No incumbent copied it quickly. Facebook bought it in April 2013 for a reported $85 million, then announced in January 2016 it would close the hosted service by January 2017 and open sourced the platform.

market_need_then: The smartphone app boom in 2011 created many small developer teams. TechCrunch in March 2012 reported over 10,000 developers signed up, growing about 40 percent month over month, mostly by word of mouth.

branding.domain_note: Operated at parse.com; the domain now redirects to parseplatform.org.

identity.voice_and_tone: Positioned in press as the Heroku of mobile; tagline the easiest way to build apps

rebrands.why: Facebook shut the hosted service and open sourced the code; the community continues under parseplatform.org

branding.community_and_virality: Developer word of mouth drove most signups; after the shutdown the open source Parse Server kept a community with docs, blog and forum.

brand_strength.rationale: Well known among mobile developers and the name outlived the company as an open source project, but no sourced evidence of a distinctive visual identity or mascot.

outcome_analysis: Parse caught the 2011 wave of mobile app developers with a free tier and word of mouth growth, raised a $5.5 million Series A led by Ignition in November 2011 and sold to Facebook in April 2013 for about $85 million. The product itself was later wound down by Facebook, which closed hosting in January 2017 after open sourcing it, so the company outcome was a strong exit but the hosted product did not survive.
notes: Funding: Wikipedia confirms $5.5M on 2011-11-09 without investors; TechCrunch names Ignition Partners as lead. One aggregator claimed a $7M round with a16z in 2012, not corroborated and not recorded. Facebook price of $85M comes from Wikipedia and secondary sources; Facebook did not officially state it. Founders' education not found. Company site redirects to parseplatform.org. Shutdown reason not stated by sources opened. Competitor list is thin because a dated 2011 search surfaced mostly later articles.
